newsitem.title: FRANCE: Angry workers fight Renault plans, Church weighs in.
newsitem.headline: Angry workers fight Renault plans, Church weighs in.

text.p: Angry Renault autoworkers staged brief strikes in several countries Friday, angered by the carmaker's decision to close a Belgian plant, and the Catholic Church said the resulting 3,100 job losses highlight the human cost of cut-throat economics and competition.

The Church offered advice from the Bible: "Treat others as you would like them to treat you," it said in a joint statement issued by the conference of French and Belgian Catholic Churches, quoting from the Gospel of Saint Luke in the Bible.

Belgian workers took their protest to the French embassy in Brussels, where they hurled the chassis of a Renault car made at the doomed Vilvoorde factory over police barricades to chants from the crowd of "Renault Stays Open."

In Spain, the government shied away from the controversy and said it decided to halt a subsidy of 2 billion pesetas ($13.8 million) it had earmarked to bolster Renault's investment in the modernisation of a Spanish factory that makes the small Renault Clio.
Renault has run into a storm of employee, trade union and political protest since revealing its plan last week to shut the plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels but was sticking by its decision.
Renault's Paris headquarters said a trade union call for a string of one-hour work stoppages in Spain and France had not caused any serious disruption.
A spokeswoman said between a quarter and a third of staff had followed strike calls in France. The biggest stoppage was in Seville in southern Spain, where turnout was about two-thirds.

Asked about Spain's decision to halt the subsidy, an industry ministry spokesman said, "The Spanish government has taken this decision because it doesn't make any sense for Spain that such a small amount of aid ... becomes the centre of controversy."

Belgian workers at the Vilvoorde plant have put down their tools since the company announced the closure last week. Staff at other carmakers in Belgium also protested in sympathy on Friday and Renault dealers gave their support by closing their doors for all or part of the day.

Despite the outrage and condemnation in Belgium -- from everyone from workers up to Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, whose political base is in Vilvoorde -- Renault boss Louis Schweitzer said the withdrawal was necessary.
"The reality is harsh, but it's the reality," he said. "If we do nothing the company will die. It's a brutal, hard and painful decision," he told Europe 1 radio.
Renault also has said that 2,700 job cuts in France are in the pipeline, but Schweitzer said restructuring should go no further than the plans so far announced.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has asked Schweitzer to meet Belgian staff representatives as soon as possible and a meeting of the company's European works council, composed of employers and employee delegates, has been scheduled for next Tuesday in Paris. The unions are planning more demonstrations for the same day.
